# Veteran Tributes
HomeView TributesRequest a TributeNewsVeterans LinksReferenceContact Us  
Neil A.Armstrong
Rank, Service Lieutenant Junior Grade O-2, U.S. Navy Veteran of: U.S. Navy 1949-1952 U.S. Naval Reserve 1952-1960 NACA 1955-1958 NASA 1958-1971 Cold War 1949-1960 Korean War 1951-1952 Tribute: Neil Armstrong was born on August 5, 1930, in Wapakoneta, Ohio. He attended Purdue University, Indiana, from 1947 until he went on active duty with the U.S. Navy on January 26, 1949. After attending flight training at NAS Pensacola, Florida, Armstrong was designated a Naval Aviator on August 12, 1950, but was not commissioned an Ensign until July 1951. His first assignment was to Fleet Aircraft Service Squadron 7 at NAS San Diego, California, from August to October 1950, followed by service as an F9F-2B Panther pilot with VF-51 from October 1950 until he left active duty and entered the Naval Reserve on August 23, 1952. During this time, he flew 78 combat missions during the Korean War flying off the aircraft carrier USS Essex (CV-9) from August 1951 to March 1952. LTJG Armstrong resigned his commission in the U.S. Naval Reserve on October 20, 1960. After leaving active duty, he completed his Bachelor of Science degree in Aerospace Engineering at Purdue in 1955, and then worked for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) at the Lewis Flight Propulsion Laboratory in Cleveland, Ohio, from February 1955 to March 1956. Armstrong next transferred to Edwards AFB, California, where he served as a NACA (NASA after July 1958) Test Pilot until he was selected for the second group of NASA Astronauts on September 16, 1962.

# Veteran Tributes
During his time at Edwards, he flew more than 50 types of aircraft and made seven flights in the X-15, reaching a top altitude of 207,500 feet and a top speed of MACH 5.74. Armstrong served as Command Pilot of Gemini 8 from March 16 to 17, 1966, and was backup Command Pilot for Gemini 11. His last mission in Space was as Commander of Apollo 11 from July 16 to 24, 1969. During this mission he became the first person to step foot on the surface of the moon on July 20, 1969. His last assignment with NASA was as Deputy Associate Administrator for Aeronautics for the Office of Advanced Research and Technology from 1970 until resigning from NASA in August 1971. After leaving NASA, Armstrong was a university professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati, Ohio, from 1971 to 1979. Neil Armstrong was awarded the Robert J. Collier Trophy and the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Nixon in 1969, the Robert H. Goddard Memorial Trophy in 1970, the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1978, and he was finally awarded his U.S. Naval Aviator Astronaut Wings in 2010. Neil Armstrong died on August 25, 2012.

# Veteran Tributes
HomeView TributesRequest a TributeNewsVeterans LinksReferenceContact Us  
Neil A.Armstrong
Rank, Service Lieutenant Junior Grade O-2, U.S. Navy Veteran of: U.S. Navy 1949-1952 U.S. Naval Reserve 1952-1960 NACA 1955-1958 NASA 1958-1971 Cold War 1949-1960 Korean War 1951-1952 Tribute: Neil Armstrong was born on August 5, 1930, in Wapakoneta, Ohio. He attended Purdue University, Indiana, from 1947 until he went on active duty with the U.S. Navy on January 26, 1949. After attending flight training at NAS Pensacola, Florida, Armstrong was designated a Naval Aviator on August 12, 1950, but was not commissioned an Ensign until July 1951. His first assignment was to Fleet Aircraft Service Squadron 7 at NAS San Diego, California, from August to October 1950, followed by service as an F9F-2B Panther pilot with VF-51 from October 1950 until he left active duty and entered the Naval Reserve on August 23, 1952. During this time, he flew 78 combat missions during the Korean War flying off the aircraft carrier USS Essex (CV-9) from August 1951 to March 1952. LTJG Armstrong resigned his commission in the U.S. Naval Reserve on October 20, 1960. After leaving active duty, he completed his Bachelor of Science degree in Aerospace Engineering at Purdue in 1955, and then worked for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA) at the Lewis Flight Propulsion Laboratory in Cleveland, Ohio, from February 1955 to March 1956. Armstrong next transferred to Edwards AFB, California, where he served as a NACA (NASA after July 1958) Test Pilot until he was selected for the second group of NASA Astronauts on September 16, 1962.

# Veteran Tributes
During his time at Edwards, he flew more than 50 types of aircraft and made seven flights in the X-15, reaching a top altitude of 207,500 feet and a top speed of MACH 5.74. Armstrong served as Command Pilot of Gemini 8 from March 16 to 17, 1966, and was backup Command Pilot for Gemini 11. His last mission in Space was as Commander of Apollo 11 from July 16 to 24, 1969. During this mission he became the first person to step foot on the surface of the moon on July 20, 1969. His last assignment with NASA was as Deputy Associate Administrator for Aeronautics for the Office of Advanced Research and Technology from 1970 until resigning from NASA in August 1971. After leaving NASA, Armstrong was a university professor of aerospace engineering at the University of Cincinnati, Ohio, from 1971 to 1979. Neil Armstrong was awarded the Robert J. Collier Trophy and the Presidential Medal of Freedom by President Nixon in 1969, the Robert H. Goddard Memorial Trophy in 1970, the Congressional Space Medal of Honor in 1978, and he was finally awarded his U.S. Naval Aviator Astronaut Wings in 2010. Neil Armstrong died on August 25, 2012.

The **Korean Armistice Agreement** (Korean: 한국정전협정; Hanja: 韓國停戰協定) is an armistice that brought about a cessation of hostilities of the Korean War. It was signed by United States ArmyLieutenant General[William Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr.") and GeneralMark W. Clark representing the United Nations Command (UNC), North Korea leader Kim Il Sung and General Nam Il representing the [Korean People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_People's_Army "Korean People's Army") (KPA), and Peng Dehuai representing the Chinese[People's Volunteer Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Volunteer_Army "People's Volunteer Army") (PVA).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-1) The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, and came into force at 22:00 local time (UTC+09:00) the same day[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-2) and was designed to "ensure a complete cessation of hostilities and of all acts of armed force in Korea until a final peaceful settlement is achieved."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
During the 1954 Geneva Conference in Switzerland, Chinese Premier and foreign minister Zhou Enlai suggested that a peace treaty should be implemented on the Korean peninsula. However, the US secretary of state, John Foster Dulles, did not accommodate this attempt to achieve such a treaty. A final peace settlement has never been achieved.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto-4) The signed armistice established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the de facto new border between the two nations, put into force a ceasefire, and finalized repatriation of prisoners of war. The DMZ runs close to the 38th parallel and has separated North and South Korea since the Korean Armistice Agreement was signed in 1953.

South Korea never signed the Armistice Agreement, due to President Syngman Rhee's refusal to accept having failed to unify Korea by force.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) China normalized relations and signed a peace treaty with South Korea in 1992. In 1994, China withdrew from the Military Armistice Commission, essentially leaving North Korea and the UN Command as the only participants in the armistice agreement.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto1-8) In 2011, South Korea stated that North Korea had violated the armistice 221 times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto2-9)
Mosaic depicting Kim Il-sung and KPA generals during Korean War

By mid-December 1950, the United States was discussing terms for an agreement to end the Korean War.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The desired agreement would end the fighting, provide assurances against its resumption, and protect the future security of UNC forces.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995211-11) The United States asked for a military armistice commission of mixed membership that would supervise all agreements.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) Both sides would need to agree to "cease the introduction into Korea of any reinforcing air, ground or naval units or personnel... and to refrain from increasing the level of war equipment and material existing in Korea."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The U.S. wished to create a demilitarized zone that would be roughly 20 miles (32 km) wide.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The proposed agreement would also address the issue of prisoners of war which the U.S. believed should be exchanged on a one-for-one basis.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10)

While talk of a possible armistice agreement was circulating, in late May and early June 1951, the President of the Republic of Korea (ROK, South Korea) Syngman Rhee opposed peace talks. He believed the ROK should continue to expand its army in order to march all the way to the Yalu River and completely unify the nation.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) The UNC did not endorse Rhee's position.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) Even without UNC support, Rhee and the South Korean government attempted to mobilize the public to resist any halt in the fighting short of the Yalu River.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) Other ROK officials supported Rhee's ambitions and the National Assembly of South Korea unanimously passed a resolution endorsing a continued fight for an "independent and unified country."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) At the end of June, however, the Assembly decided to support armistice talks,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) although President Rhee continued to oppose them.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-13)

A major, problematic negotiation point was the repatriation of prisoners-of-war.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990187%E2%80%9399-23) The Communists held 10,000, and the UNC held 150,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The PVA, KPA, and UNC could not agree on a system of repatriation because many PVA and KPA soldiers refused to be repatriated to the north,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-Boose2000-24) which was unacceptable to the Chinese and North Koreans.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990189%E2%80%9390-25) In the final armistice agreement, signed on 27 July 1953, a Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, chaired by Indian General K. S. Thimayya, was set up to handle the matter.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury199024%E2%80%9345-26)

In 1952, the United States elected a new president, Dwight D. Eisenhower. On 2 December 1952,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-27) he went to Korea to investigate what might end the war.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990240-28)Kenneth Nichols wrote that President Eisenhower "ended the Korean hostilities by discreetly threatening to use atomic weapons if the North Koreans and the Chinese did not agree to a cessation of hostilities".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTENichols198712-29) With the UN accepting India's proposed NNPC POW exchange framework,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-30) the KPA, PVA, and UNC ceased fire with the battle line approximately at the Kansas Line, a line of UN positions north of the 38th parallel, which had been established in Operation Rugged.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-31) Upon agreeing to the armistice, the belligerents established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which has since been patrolled by KPA, ROKA, United States, and Joint UNC forces. Discussions continued slowly because of difficulties regarding demarcation of the border between North and South Korea. China and North Korea expected the line to remain at the 38th parallel. Within weeks, however, both nations accepted the Kansas Line.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) In March 1953, the death of Joseph Stalin helped spur negotiations.

While the Chinese leader Mao Zedong was not then willing to compromise, the new Soviet leadership issued a statement two weeks after Stalin's death, which called for a quick end to hostilities.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgov2013238-32)
The building in which the armistice was signed now houses the North Korea Peace Museum.
On 19 July 1953, the delegates reached agreement covering all issues on the agenda.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-33) On 27 July 1953, at 10:00 a.m., the Armistice was signed by Nam Il, a delegate of the KPA and PVA, and [William K. Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr."), a UNC delegate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) Twelve hours after the signing of the document, all regulations that were approved in the armistice went into effect.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2000322-34) The agreement provided for monitoring by an international commission. The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC) was established to prevent reinforcements being brought into Korea, whether additional military personnel or new weapons, and NNSC member inspection teams from Czechoslovakia, Poland, Sweden, and Switzerland operated throughout Korea.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995216-14)
The Demilitarized Zone compared to the earlier 38th parallel de facto border

A key feature of the armistice is that no nation is a signatory to the agreement; it is purely a military document.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-cafunc-35) The signed Armistice established a "complete cessation of all hostilities in Korea by all armed forces",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) which was to be enforced by the commanders of both sides. The armistice is, however, only a ceasefire between military forces, rather than an agreement between governments to normalize relations.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-seoul-usembassy-60th-36) No formal peace treaty was signed, and normalized relations were not restored. The armistice established the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) and the DMZ. The DMZ was agreed as a 2.5-mile -wide (4.0 km) fortified buffer zone between the two Korean nations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) The DMZ follows the Kansas Line, where the two sides actually confronted each other at the time of the signing of the Armistice. The DMZ is currently the most heavily defended national border in the world as of 2018._[citation needed_]
The Armistice also established regulations regarding prisoners-of-war. The agreement stated:
> Within sixty (60) days after this agreement becomes effective each side shall, without offering any hindrance, directly repatriate and hand over in groups all those prisoners of war in its custody who insist on repatriation to the side to which they belonged at the time of capture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
Kim Il Sung signs the agreement

Ultimately, more than 22,000 KPA or PVA soldiers refused repatriation. On the opposite side, only 327 South Korean soldiers, 21 American soldiers, and 1 British soldier also refused repatriation and remained in North Korea or in China. (See list of American and British defectors in the Korean War.)
With the signing of the Armistice, the war ended. Despite the three-year war, the international border remained at a similar location as from before the war.

texts.1:
The **Korean Armistice Agreement** (Korean: 한국정전협정; Hanja: 韓國停戰協定) is an armistice that brought about a cessation of hostilities of the Korean War. It was signed by United States ArmyLieutenant General[William Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr.") and GeneralMark W. Clark representing the United Nations Command (UNC), North Korea leader Kim Il Sung and General Nam Il representing the [Korean People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_People's_Army "Korean People's Army") (KPA), and Peng Dehuai representing the Chinese[People's Volunteer Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Volunteer_Army "People's Volunteer Army") (PVA).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-1) The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, and came into force at 22:00 local time (UTC+09:00) the same day[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-2) and was designed to "ensure a complete cessation of hostilities and of all acts of armed force in Korea until a final peaceful settlement is achieved."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
During the 1954 Geneva Conference in Switzerland, Chinese Premier and foreign minister Zhou Enlai suggested that a peace treaty should be implemented on the Korean peninsula. However, the US secretary of state, John Foster Dulles, did not accommodate this attempt to achieve such a treaty. A final peace settlement has never been achieved.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto-4) The signed armistice established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the de facto new border between the two nations, put into force a ceasefire, and finalized repatriation of prisoners of war. The DMZ runs close to the 38th parallel and has separated North and South Korea since the Korean Armistice Agreement was signed in 1953.
texts.2:
South Korea never signed the Armistice Agreement, due to President Syngman Rhee's refusal to accept having failed to unify Korea by force.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) China normalized relations and signed a peace treaty with South Korea in 1992. In 1994, China withdrew from the Military Armistice Commission, essentially leaving North Korea and the UN Command as the only participants in the armistice agreement.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto1-8) In 2011, South Korea stated that North Korea had violated the armistice 221 times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto2-9)
Mosaic depicting Kim Il-sung and KPA generals during Korean War
texts.3: By mid-December 1950, the United States was discussing terms for an agreement to end the Korean War.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The desired agreement would end the fighting, provide assurances against its resumption, and protect the future security of UNC forces.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995211-11) The United States asked for a military armistice commission of mixed membership that would supervise all agreements.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) Both sides would need to agree to "cease the introduction into Korea of any reinforcing air, ground or naval units or personnel... and to refrain from increasing the level of war equipment and material existing in Korea."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The U.S. wished to create a demilitarized zone that would be roughly 20 miles (32 km) wide.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The proposed agreement would also address the issue of prisoners of war which the U.S. believed should be exchanged on a one-for-one basis.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10)
texts.4: While talk of a possible armistice agreement was circulating, in late May and early June 1951, the President of the Republic of Korea (ROK, South Korea) Syngman Rhee opposed peace talks. He believed the ROK should continue to expand its army in order to march all the way to the Yalu River and completely unify the nation.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) The UNC did not endorse Rhee's position.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) Even without UNC support, Rhee and the South Korean government attempted to mobilize the public to resist any halt in the fighting short of the Yalu River.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) Other ROK officials supported Rhee's ambitions and the National Assembly of South Korea unanimously passed a resolution endorsing a continued fight for an "independent and unified country."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) At the end of June, however, the Assembly decided to support armistice talks,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) although President Rhee continued to oppose them.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-13)
texts.8: A major, problematic negotiation point was the repatriation of prisoners-of-war.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990187%E2%80%9399-23) The Communists held 10,000, and the UNC held 150,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The PVA, KPA, and UNC could not agree on a system of repatriation because many PVA and KPA soldiers refused to be repatriated to the north,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-Boose2000-24) which was unacceptable to the Chinese and North Koreans.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990189%E2%80%9390-25) In the final armistice agreement, signed on 27 July 1953, a Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, chaired by Indian General K. S. Thimayya, was set up to handle the matter.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury199024%E2%80%9345-26)
texts.9: In 1952, the United States elected a new president, Dwight D. Eisenhower. On 2 December 1952,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-27) he went to Korea to investigate what might end the war.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990240-28)Kenneth Nichols wrote that President Eisenhower "ended the Korean hostilities by discreetly threatening to use atomic weapons if the North Koreans and the Chinese did not agree to a cessation of hostilities".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTENichols198712-29) With the UN accepting India's proposed NNPC POW exchange framework,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-30) the KPA, PVA, and UNC ceased fire with the battle line approximately at the Kansas Line, a line of UN positions north of the 38th parallel, which had been established in Operation Rugged.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-31) Upon agreeing to the armistice, the belligerents established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which has since been patrolled by KPA, ROKA, United States, and Joint UNC forces. Discussions continued slowly because of difficulties regarding demarcation of the border between North and South Korea. China and North Korea expected the line to remain at the 38th parallel. Within weeks, however, both nations accepted the Kansas Line.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) In March 1953, the death of Joseph Stalin helped spur negotiations.
texts.10:
While the Chinese leader Mao Zedong was not then willing to compromise, the new Soviet leadership issued a statement two weeks after Stalin's death, which called for a quick end to hostilities.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgov2013238-32)
The building in which the armistice was signed now houses the North Korea Peace Museum.
On 19 July 1953, the delegates reached agreement covering all issues on the agenda.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-33) On 27 July 1953, at 10:00 a.m., the Armistice was signed by Nam Il, a delegate of the KPA and PVA, and [William K. Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr."), a UNC delegate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) Twelve hours after the signing of the document, all regulations that were approved in the armistice went into effect.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2000322-34) The agreement provided for monitoring by an international commission. The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC) was established to prevent reinforcements being brought into Korea, whether additional military personnel or new weapons, and NNSC member inspection teams from Czechoslovakia, Poland, Sweden, and Switzerland operated throughout Korea.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995216-14)
The Demilitarized Zone compared to the earlier 38th parallel de facto border
texts.11:
A key feature of the armistice is that no nation is a signatory to the agreement; it is purely a military document.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-cafunc-35) The signed Armistice established a "complete cessation of all hostilities in Korea by all armed forces",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) which was to be enforced by the commanders of both sides. The armistice is, however, only a ceasefire between military forces, rather than an agreement between governments to normalize relations.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-seoul-usembassy-60th-36) No formal peace treaty was signed, and normalized relations were not restored. The armistice established the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) and the DMZ. The DMZ was agreed as a 2.5-mile -wide (4.0 km) fortified buffer zone between the two Korean nations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) The DMZ follows the Kansas Line, where the two sides actually confronted each other at the time of the signing of the Armistice. The DMZ is currently the most heavily defended national border in the world as of 2018._[citation needed_]
The Armistice also established regulations regarding prisoners-of-war. The agreement stated:
> Within sixty (60) days after this agreement becomes effective each side shall, without offering any hindrance, directly repatriate and hand over in groups all those prisoners of war in its custody who insist on repatriation to the side to which they belonged at the time of capture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
Kim Il Sung signs the agreement
texts.12:
Ultimately, more than 22,000 KPA or PVA soldiers refused repatriation. On the opposite side, only 327 South Korean soldiers, 21 American soldiers, and 1 British soldier also refused repatriation and remained in North Korea or in China. (See list of American and British defectors in the Korean War.)
With the signing of the Armistice, the war ended. Despite the three-year war, the international border remained at a similar location as from before the war.

The **Korean Armistice Agreement** (Korean: 한국정전협정; Hanja: 韓國停戰協定) is an armistice that brought about a cessation of hostilities of the Korean War. It was signed by United States ArmyLieutenant General[William Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr.") and GeneralMark W. Clark representing the United Nations Command (UNC), North Korea leader Kim Il Sung and General Nam Il representing the [Korean People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_People's_Army "Korean People's Army") (KPA), and Peng Dehuai representing the Chinese[People's Volunteer Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Volunteer_Army "People's Volunteer Army") (PVA).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-1) The armistice was signed on 27 July 1953, and came into force at 22:00 local time (UTC+09:00) the same day[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-2) and was designed to "ensure a complete cessation of hostilities and of all acts of armed force in Korea until a final peaceful settlement is achieved."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
During the 1954 Geneva Conference in Switzerland, Chinese Premier and foreign minister Zhou Enlai suggested that a peace treaty should be implemented on the Korean peninsula. However, the US secretary of state, John Foster Dulles, did not accommodate this attempt to achieve such a treaty. A final peace settlement has never been achieved.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto-4) The signed armistice established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), the de facto new border between the two nations, put into force a ceasefire, and finalized repatriation of prisoners of war. The DMZ runs close to the 38th parallel and has separated North and South Korea since the Korean Armistice Agreement was signed in 1953.

South Korea never signed the Armistice Agreement, due to President Syngman Rhee's refusal to accept having failed to unify Korea by force.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) China normalized relations and signed a peace treaty with South Korea in 1992. In 1994, China withdrew from the Military Armistice Commission, essentially leaving North Korea and the UN Command as the only participants in the armistice agreement.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto1-8) In 2011, South Korea stated that North Korea had violated the armistice 221 times.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-auto2-9)
Mosaic depicting Kim Il-sung and KPA generals during Korean War

By mid-December 1950, the United States was discussing terms for an agreement to end the Korean War.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The desired agreement would end the fighting, provide assurances against its resumption, and protect the future security of UNC forces.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995211-11) The United States asked for a military armistice commission of mixed membership that would supervise all agreements.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) Both sides would need to agree to "cease the introduction into Korea of any reinforcing air, ground or naval units or personnel... and to refrain from increasing the level of war equipment and material existing in Korea."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The U.S. wished to create a demilitarized zone that would be roughly 20 miles (32 km) wide.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The proposed agreement would also address the issue of prisoners of war which the U.S. believed should be exchanged on a one-for-one basis.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10)

While talk of a possible armistice agreement was circulating, in late May and early June 1951, the President of the Republic of Korea (ROK, South Korea) Syngman Rhee opposed peace talks. He believed the ROK should continue to expand its army in order to march all the way to the Yalu River and completely unify the nation.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) The UNC did not endorse Rhee's position.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995214-6) Even without UNC support, Rhee and the South Korean government attempted to mobilize the public to resist any halt in the fighting short of the Yalu River.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) Other ROK officials supported Rhee's ambitions and the National Assembly of South Korea unanimously passed a resolution endorsing a continued fight for an "independent and unified country."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) At the end of June, however, the Assembly decided to support armistice talks,[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995215-12) although President Rhee continued to oppose them.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-13)

A major, problematic negotiation point was the repatriation of prisoners-of-war.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990187%E2%80%9399-23) The Communists held 10,000, and the UNC held 150,000.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995212-10) The PVA, KPA, and UNC could not agree on a system of repatriation because many PVA and KPA soldiers refused to be repatriated to the north,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-Boose2000-24) which was unacceptable to the Chinese and North Koreans.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990189%E2%80%9390-25) In the final armistice agreement, signed on 27 July 1953, a Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission, chaired by Indian General K. S. Thimayya, was set up to handle the matter.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury199024%E2%80%9345-26)

In 1952, the United States elected a new president, Dwight D. Eisenhower. On 2 December 1952,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-27) he went to Korea to investigate what might end the war.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStokesbury1990240-28)Kenneth Nichols wrote that President Eisenhower "ended the Korean hostilities by discreetly threatening to use atomic weapons if the North Koreans and the Chinese did not agree to a cessation of hostilities".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTENichols198712-29) With the UN accepting India's proposed NNPC POW exchange framework,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-30) the KPA, PVA, and UNC ceased fire with the battle line approximately at the Kansas Line, a line of UN positions north of the 38th parallel, which had been established in Operation Rugged.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-31) Upon agreeing to the armistice, the belligerents established the Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which has since been patrolled by KPA, ROKA, United States, and Joint UNC forces. Discussions continued slowly because of difficulties regarding demarcation of the border between North and South Korea. China and North Korea expected the line to remain at the 38th parallel. Within weeks, however, both nations accepted the Kansas Line.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) In March 1953, the death of Joseph Stalin helped spur negotiations.

While the Chinese leader Mao Zedong was not then willing to compromise, the new Soviet leadership issued a statement two weeks after Stalin's death, which called for a quick end to hostilities.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAgov2013238-32)
The building in which the armistice was signed now houses the North Korea Peace Museum.
On 19 July 1953, the delegates reached agreement covering all issues on the agenda.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-33) On 27 July 1953, at 10:00 a.m., the Armistice was signed by Nam Il, a delegate of the KPA and PVA, and [William K. Harrison Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kelly_Harrison_Jr. "William Kelly Harrison Jr."), a UNC delegate.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) Twelve hours after the signing of the document, all regulations that were approved in the armistice went into effect.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTECatchpole2000322-34) The agreement provided for monitoring by an international commission. The Neutral Nations Supervisory Commission (NNSC) was established to prevent reinforcements being brought into Korea, whether additional military personnel or new weapons, and NNSC member inspection teams from Czechoslovakia, Poland, Sweden, and Switzerland operated throughout Korea.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStueck1995216-14)
The Demilitarized Zone compared to the earlier 38th parallel de facto border

A key feature of the armistice is that no nation is a signatory to the agreement; it is purely a military document.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-cafunc-35) The signed Armistice established a "complete cessation of all hostilities in Korea by all armed forces",[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3) which was to be enforced by the commanders of both sides. The armistice is, however, only a ceasefire between military forces, rather than an agreement between governments to normalize relations.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-seoul-usembassy-60th-36) No formal peace treaty was signed, and normalized relations were not restored. The armistice established the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) and the DMZ. The DMZ was agreed as a 2.5-mile -wide (4.0 km) fortified buffer zone between the two Korean nations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMountLaferriere2004123-15) The DMZ follows the Kansas Line, where the two sides actually confronted each other at the time of the signing of the Armistice. The DMZ is currently the most heavily defended national border in the world as of 2018._[citation needed_]
The Armistice also established regulations regarding prisoners-of-war. The agreement stated:
> Within sixty (60) days after this agreement becomes effective each side shall, without offering any hindrance, directly repatriate and hand over in groups all those prisoners of war in its custody who insist on repatriation to the side to which they belonged at the time of capture.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Armistice_Agreement#cite_note-findlaw-19530727-3)
Kim Il Sung signs the agreement

Ultimately, more than 22,000 KPA or PVA soldiers refused repatriation. On the opposite side, only 327 South Korean soldiers, 21 American soldiers, and 1 British soldier also refused repatriation and remained in North Korea or in China. (See list of American and British defectors in the Korean War.)
With the signing of the Armistice, the war ended. Despite the three-year war, the international border remained at a similar location as from before the war.
